title: Blog 1
content:
EC2 AMI TAG SHARING: SHARING EC2 AMI TAGS ACROSS AWS ACCOUNTS Summary, analysis, and hands-on lab based on the original article “Introducing EC2 AMI Tag Sharing: Share EC2 tags across AWS accounts” (AWS Compute Blog, Oct 05, 2026, by Gena Gizzi and Smriti Ohri).
Source: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/introducing-ec2-ami-tag-sharing-share-ec2-tags-across-aws-accounts/
1. Background: Tags and AMIs Tags are key-value pairs attached to AWS resources. They are widely used for cost tracking (FinOps), compliance auditing (Security), and attribute-based access control (ABAC).
AMIs (Amazon Machine Images) serve as templates used to launch EC2 instances. Many organizations tag their AMIs to record approval status, operating system version, owning team, and compliance levels.
2. Previous Challenges Previously, when sharing an AMI with other AWS accounts, tags did not carry over with the image. Recipient accounts could see and launch the image, but could not see any metadata describing it. To bridge this gap, organizations had to build and maintain custom tag replication mechanisms, typically combining Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and AWS Lambda across accounts. This approach presented three major drawbacks:
Required provisioning, configuring, and maintaining additional infrastructure. The volume of CreateTags API calls spiked dramatically with numerous AMIs across multiple Regions and accounts, causing API throttling or Lambda execution failures. Risk of tag drift whenever an asynchronous Lambda execution silently failed without compensatory retry mechanisms. 3. What is EC2 AMI Tag Sharing? EC2 AMI Tag Sharing allows AMI owners to share tags directly with the AMI across all accounts that have access permissions (shared privately with specific accounts, across an AWS Organization, or publicly).
Usage is straightforward: prefix the tag key with ec2:SharedTag/.
Tag Key Visibility ec2:SharedTag/status AMI owner and all accounts with access to the shared AMI team (no prefix) AMI owner only (private tag) Key rules to remember:
Only the AMI owner can create, modify, or delete tags with the ec2:SharedTag/ prefix. Recipient accounts have read-only access to shared tags, but can still attach their own private tags to the shared AMI. When the owner updates a shared tag, the update is automatically reflected across all recipient accounts without custom automation. Shared tags count toward the owner’s quota of 50 tags per resource, not toward the recipient’s quota. When copying an AMI with shared tags, the Copy tags parameter (--copy-image-tags in CLI) must be specified to duplicate tags. Currently, this feature only supports AMI resources, and does not apply to EBS Snapshots. 4. Primary Use Case: Golden AMI Pipeline In enterprise multi-account architectures, organizations often establish a central build-factory account to package hardened, pre-configured AMIs (Golden AMIs) and share them with dozens or hundreds of workload accounts. These workload accounts enforce IAM policies or SCPs allowing instances to launch only from AMIs with valid approval tags:
Criteria Previously With EC2 AMI Tag Sharing Synchronization EventBridge triggers SNS, invoking Lambda in each target account to call CreateTags Owner simply attaches tags prefixed with ec2:SharedTag/ once Updating status (e.g. marking deprecated) Pipeline must re-trigger across all recipient accounts New value is instantly reflected in all recipient accounts natively Reliability & Overhead Susceptible to API throttling, Lambda failures, and tag drift Native AWS platform feature with zero maintenance overhead 5. Key Considerations Do not store sensitive data in shared tags: Any account with access to the AMI can inspect all shared tags. Recipient ABAC policies apply to shared tags: If an IAM policy restricts ec2:RunInstances to AMIs where status=approved, the tag ec2:SharedTag/status=approved satisfies that policy condition. Control resides with the AMI owner: Recipient accounts cannot alter shared tag values, so recipient accounts should only trust AMIs from verified internal builder accounts. Combine with Allowed AMIs: Use the Allowed AMIs feature to restrict instance launch permissions strictly to trusted internal accounts. 6. Hands-on Implementation Environment: Region: us-east-1 (US East - N. Virginia). Base Instance: blog1-ami-tag-lab, instance type t3.micro / t2.micro (Free Tier), running Amazon Linux 2023 (al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64). Tool: AWS Management Console (EC2 interface). Execution Steps: Launched a baseline EC2 instance running Amazon Linux 2023. Created the source AMI blog1-ami-tag-lab-origin. Assigned shared tags (ec2:SharedTag/status=approved, ec2:SharedTag/os-version=al2023) and a private tag (team=blog1-lab). Filtered and verified tags on the AWS Console: Used the Filter AMI by attribute or tag search bar with ec2:SharedTag/status, correctly matching the created AMI. Updated Shared Tag value: Simulated deprecating the AMI by navigating to Manage tags and changing ec2:SharedTag/status from approved to deprecated. Tested AMI Copy behavior: Copy 1 (blog1-copy-with-tags): Enabled Copy tags ➔ Result: All tags (shared and private) were duplicated to the new AMI. Copy 2 (blog1-copy-without-tags): Disabled Copy tags ➔ Result: The new AMI was created with no tags attached. Cleaned up resources: Deregistered all 3 AMIs, deleted all associated EBS Snapshots, and terminated the base instance to avoid unwanted storage charges. Observations: Console filtering seamlessly handles the ec2:SharedTag/* prefix, simplifying AMI governance across distributed teams. The Copy tags flag is critical when copying AMIs across Regions; omitting it strips all metadata and risks breaking ABAC policies in destination Regions. Encountered Issues & Solutions: Issue: When creating the image with the default “Tag image and snapshots together” option, AWS returned an error: Failed to create image: Tag key with shared tag prefix 'ec2:SharedTag/' is not supported for resource type 'snapshot'. Cause & Resolution: EC2 AMI Tag Sharing currently only supports AMI resources, not EBS Snapshots. This was resolved by choosing “Tag image and snapshots separately”, applying ec2:SharedTag/ keys exclusively to the Image tags section and leaving the Snapshot tags section empty or with standard tags. Figure 1: Tags tab of source AMI displaying Shared Tags and private tag
Figure 2: Filtering AMIs by ec2:SharedTag/status on AWS Console
Figure 3: Copied AMI with Copy tags enabled preserving all tags
Figure 4: Copied AMI with Copy tags disabled possessing no tags
7. Personal Insights Operational Excellence & FinOps:
Previously, keeping tags in sync across accounts in a Golden AMI pipeline required maintaining an event-driven mesh of EventBridge rules, SNS topics, and cross-account Lambda functions. This incurred operational cost, introduced throttling risks at scale, and caused tag drift when executions failed silently. Native support for ec2:SharedTag/ eliminates this entire middleware layer with instantaneous synchronization and zero maintenance. Security & Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC):
Enforcing read-only access for recipient accounts safeguards metadata integrity. However, it establishes a tight trust boundary with the owner account: if the owner account is compromised or unintentionally marks an unvetted image as approved, recipient accounts with tag-dependent IAM policies could inadvertently launch insecure workloads. Organizations should layer this with Allowed AMIs and AWS Organizations SCPs for defense in depth. Enterprise Recommendations:
For production Golden AMI workflows, standardizing on the following shared tags is highly recommended: ec2:SharedTag/status: Values approved | testing | deprecated to govern instance launch permissions via IAM. ec2:SharedTag/os-version: Identifies the standardized OS distribution (e.g., al2023, ubuntu-22.04). ec2:SharedTag/patch-date: Captures the latest patch baseline date for automated SecOps compliance scans. ec2:SharedTag/compliance-tier: Designates security benchmarks (e.g., pci-dss, cis-benchmark-l1). 8. References Introducing EC2 AMI Tag Sharing: Share EC2 tags across AWS accounts (AWS Compute Blog) Tag your Amazon EC2 resources (EC2 User Guide) Allowed AMIs (EC2 User Guide) AWS Study Group post: (Updating with post URL)

Practice: + Task 1 (EC2): launch an instance named Test Instance, create the key pair first-kp (RSA, .pem), create a security group, connect via SSH, attach an EBS volume, then terminate the instance + Task 2 (Bedrock): submit the use case, select Claude Haiku 5.5, run a test prompt in the Playground + Task 4 (Lambda): create the function http-function-url-tutorial from the “Getting started with Lambda HTTP” blueprint, check the function URL, then delete the function + Task 5 (RDS): create an Aurora (PostgreSQL Compatible) database with Easy create, wait for the Available status, then delete the instance and cluster - Review all resources to make sure everything has been cleaned up - Check the Credits page in Billing to confirm the credits received 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 https://000001.awsfcaj.com/ Practice task details: Task 1: Launch an EC2 instance Open the task “Launch an instance using EC2” in the Explore AWS widget on the Console Home, then choose Start activity. Name the instance, choose an AMI, and keep the default hardware configuration. Create a new key pair (name first-kp, type RSA, format .pem) and store the key file safely for later SSH use. Create a new security group with the default options, review the configuration, then choose Launch instance. After completing the task, terminate the instance to avoid incurring costs. Task 2: Amazon Bedrock Playground Select the task “Use a foundation model in the Amazon Bedrock”, choose the Claude Haiku 5.5 model, and fill in the use case details. If you get an error about not having access to the model, create a support case (Account and billing → Account Activation → Bedrock Allowlisting) with your Account ID and Region, then wait for AWS to respond. Once access is granted, enter a test prompt, run it, and review the model’s response. Task 3: AWS Budgets Select the task “Set up a cost budget using AWS Budgets”. Enter the email to receive notifications, create the budget, and verify it was created successfully. This is an important step for tracking costs and avoiding exceeding the credit limit. Task 4: Web app with AWS Lambda Select the task “Create a web app using AWS Lambda” and use the Getting started with Lambda HTTP blueprint. Name the function http-function-url-tutorial, accept the acknowledgment, and create the function. After finishing, delete the function (enter confirm to confirm). Task 5: Database with Amazon RDS Select the task “Create an Amazon RDS Database” and use Easy create with the Aurora (PostgreSQL Compatible) engine. Wait for the database to reach the Available status. Clean up: delete the DB instance (database-1-instance-1), then delete the DB cluster (database-1), uncheck creating a final snapshot, and enter delete me to confirm. Compute Storage Networking Database … Understood the structure of AWS global infrastructure (Region, Availability Zone, Edge Location) and the Shared Responsibility Model.

Check account & configuration information Retrieve the list of regions View EC2 service Create and manage key pairs Check information about running services … Gained solid foundational knowledge of EC2: instance types, AMI, EBS, key pair, security group, Elastic IP, and SSH connection methods.
Completed the practice tasks of the AWS Free Tier program:
EC2: launched an instance, connected via SSH, attached an EBS volume, and terminated it after use. Amazon Bedrock: experimented with a foundation model (Claude Haiku 5.5) in the Playground. Acquired the ability to connect between the web interface and CLI to manage AWS resources in parallel.

title: Week 2 Worklog
content:
Week 2 Objectives: Understand the role of cost management when operating systems on AWS and get to know the AWS Budgets service. Distinguish the 4 budget types: Cost Budget, Usage Budget, RI Budget, and Savings Plans Budget. Practice creating a budget from a template and a customized budget in AWS Billing and Cost Management, and configure email alert thresholds. Learn about the AWS Support plans (Basic, Business Support+, Enterprise Support, Unified Operations) and their response times. Understand the process of accessing AWS Support Center, creating and managing support requests, and choosing an appropriate severity level. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Learn the overview of AWS Budgets: + Purpose: set budgets and send alerts when costs exceed (or are forecasted to exceed) the allowance + 4 budget types: Cost, Usage, RI, Savings Plans + Benefits: cost control, timely alerts, financial planning, resource optimization, cost allocation - Learn the steps to set up budgets effectively: define goals, analyze current costs, set alert thresholds (typically 80% and 100%), configure notifications, monitor and adjust - Distinguish Reserved Instances from Savings Plans 12/10/2026 12/10/2026 https://000007.awsfcaj.com/ 3 - Practice: + Go to AWS Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create a budget + Create a budget from a template: choose Use a template (simplified) → Monthly cost budget, set the name, monthly amount, and alert thresholds + View budget history and the alert types available in the template + Create a customized Cost Budget: name it Monthly, choose Period, Recurring/Expiring, Fixed/Monthly Budget Planning, enter the Budgeted amount, scope All AWS services, Unblended costs, add an alert threshold 13/10/2026 13/10/2026 https://000007.awsfcaj.com/1-create-budget/ https://000007.awsfcaj.com/2-cost-budgets/ 4 - Practice: + Create a Usage Budget: choose Usage type groups, EC2: ELB - Running Hours, set the running-hours limit, configure the alert threshold and email + View Budget health and Budget history + Review the process of creating an RI Budget (Reservation budget) and a Savings Plans Budget (demonstration only, since they require upfront payment/long-term commitment) + Clean up: select a budget → Actions → Delete → confirm deletion, repeat for all created budgets 14/10/2026 14/10/2026 https://000007.awsfcaj.com/3-usage-budget/ https://000007.awsfcaj.com/4-reservation-budget/ https://000007.awsfcaj.com/5-saving-plans-budget/ https://000007.awsfcaj.com/6-clean-up/ 5 - Learn about AWS Support and its support plans: + Basic + Business Support+ + Enterprise Support + Unified Operations - Compare the features and response times of each plan - Learn how to access AWS Support: support request types and the process of changing a support plan 15/10/2026 15/10/2026 https://000009.awsfcaj.com/ https://000009.awsfcaj.com/1-support-plans/ https://000009.awsfcaj.com/2-access-support/ 6 - Learn how to manage support requests in AWS Support Center: + Create a support request + Select an appropriate severity level + Track and respond to requests - Take note of the security considerations when creating a support case - Summarize week 2 knowledge and write the worklog 16/10/2026 16/10/2026 https://000009.awsfcaj.com/3-manage-cases/ Practice and learning details: Lab 7: Cost Management with AWS Budgets 1. AWS Budgets overview
AWS Budgets lets you set budgets and send alerts when costs exceed the allowance (or are forecasted to exceed it). Four budget types: Cost Budget: sends alerts when total costs exceed the threshold. Usage Budget: sends alerts when usage of the selected service exceeds the threshold (for example, EC2 running hours). RI Budget: sends alerts based on the usage of prepaid Reserved Instances. Savings Plans Budget: sends alerts based on the usage of services covered by Savings Plans. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are both ways to reduce costs by committing to usage for 1 - 3 years. Savings Plans is the newer, more flexible model with equivalent discounts; for EC2, Savings Plans is recommended. Benefits: proactive cost control, timely alerts, support for financial planning and cost forecasting, identifying high-cost services to optimize, and easy cost allocation to projects/departments/customers. Steps to set up budgets effectively: (1) define budget goals, (2) analyze current costs, (3) set appropriate alert thresholds (typically 80% and 100%), (4) configure notifications to the right authorized people, (5) monitor and adjust regularly. 2. Create a budget using a template
Open the AWS Management Console and find AWS Billing and Cost Management. Choose Budgets from the left menu, then click Create a budget. Select Use a template (simplified), then under Templates choose Monthly cost budget. Enter the budget name, monthly budget amount, and alert thresholds, then click Create budget. Verify the budget was created, and view the budget history and the alert types available in the template. Note: budget alerts only notify, they do not automatically stop resources when the budget is exceeded; combine with AWS Service Quotas or IAM policies to control usage. Set proper permissions so only authorized personnel can edit or delete budgets. 3. Create a Cost Budget (Customize)
Note: new AWS accounts may initially only be able to create a Cost Budget; other budget types may not be available right away. In Budget setup choose Customize, under Budget types choose Cost budget, then click Next. In Set your budget: Budget name: Monthly Period: Daily / Monthly / Quarterly / Annually Budget effective dates: Recurring Budget (repeats periodically) or Expiring Budget (applies only once). AWS Budgets uses the UTC time zone. Specify your monthly budget: Fixed (same amount each period) or Monthly Budget Planning (different amounts per month); enter the Budgeted amount. Budget scope: choose All AWS services; Aggregate costs by: Unblended costs; click Next. Configure alerts: choose Add an alert threshold, set the alert details, click Next; review the actions (if any), click Next. Review all settings, click Create budget, and confirm the budget was created successfully. Recommendation: set multiple alert thresholds (for example 50%, 80%, 100%) to control costs proactively. 4. Create a Usage Budget
The process is similar to a Cost Budget, with one main difference: a Usage Budget works on resource usage rather than cost. In Budget setup choose Customize, under Budget types choose Usage budget, then click Next. Enter the Budget name; under Budget against choose Usage type groups and select EC2: ELB - Running Hours to monitor EC2 running hours. Configure Set budget amount: Period (Daily/Monthly/Quarterly/Annually), Budget renewal type (Recurring/Expiring), Budgeting method (Fixed/Planned), and the maximum usage hours. Keep the defaults in Budget scope and click Next. In Configure alerts: choose Add an alert threshold, set the threshold (% of budget), add the email to receive notifications, and click Next. Review and click Create budget. After creation, view Budget health to compare current usage against the budget and Budget history to track trends. Especially useful for hourly-billed services like EC2. Only send notifications to the people responsible for cost management to avoid leaking financial information. 5. Create an RI Budget (demonstration)
Because Reserved Instances require upfront payment, this part is for demonstration only. In Budget setup choose Customize → Reservation budget → Next. Set the budget name, configure the Coverage threshold, and configure the Budget scope. In Alert setting enter the email, choose Next, then Create budget. Purpose: monitor Reserved Instance utilization to save costs; set appropriate alert thresholds to optimize usage. 6. Create a Savings Plans Budget (demonstration)
The process is very similar to an RI Budget; the difference is that a Reservation Budget relates to Reserved Instances while a Savings Plans Budget relates to Savings Plans commitments. In Budget setup choose Customize → Savings Plans budget → Next. Enter the Budget name, configure the Utilization threshold, keep the default Budget scope, enter the email in Alert setting, choose Next, then Create budget. Savings Plans can save up to 72% compared to On-Demand pricing in exchange for committing to a consistent amount of compute usage (USD/hour) for 1 or 3 years. Setting alert thresholds at 80-90% gives time to adjust. 7. Clean up resources
Go to AWS Billing and Cost Management → Budgets. Select the budget to delete → Action → Delete → click Delete in the confirmation dialog. Repeat for all budgets created during practice. Deleting a budget does not affect running resources, since budgets are only monitoring and alerting tools. Lab 9: Request Support with AWS Support 1. AWS Support plans
AWS Support is divided into 4 plans, ordered from low to high: Basic → Business Support+ → Enterprise Support → Unified Operations. Higher plans include the services of the lower plans.
Plan Key characteristics Basic - Free for all AWS customers - Support for account and billing issues, service limit increase requests - 24/7 access to: 1-on-1 live chat for account and billing questions, AWS Support Forums, AWS Health Dashboard, documentation and best practice guides Business Support+ - Designed for production workloads - 24/7 phone, chat, and email access to Cloud Support Engineers - Unlimited support cases with unlimited contacts - AWS Trusted Advisor with full checks (cost optimization, security, fault tolerance, performance, service limits) - AWS Support API - Third-party software support (common operating systems, platforms, application stack components) - Response times: general guidance < 24 hours; system impaired < 12 hours; production system impaired < 4 hours; production system down < 1 hour Enterprise Support - Includes all Business Support+ features - Technical Account Manager (TAM) - Concierge Support Team for billing and account assistance - Infrastructure Event Management - Well-Architected Reviews - Operations Reviews and Tools - Training and Game Days - Business-critical system down: response < 15 minutes; other severity levels same as Business Support+ Unified Operations - Includes all Enterprise Support features - AWS Managed Services (AMS) - 24/7 proactive monitoring and incident management - Change management - Patch management - Backup and disaster recovery - Continuous security and compliance monitoring - Dedicated service delivery team Choose a support plan that fits the technical requirements and resources of your environment; the plan also affects access to security consulting and compliance services from the AWS team. Response times range from 15 minutes to 24 hours depending on the support plan and severity; AWS Support offers multilingual support with global coverage. 2. Access AWS Support
Learn about the support request types and the process of changing a support plan. Choosing the right plan helps optimize operating costs while ensuring the necessary level of support for critical workloads. 3. Manage support requests
AWS Support Center is the centralized place to create, manage, and track all support requests. Providing detailed and complete information when creating a request helps the AWS team resolve issues faster. Security: do not share access keys, passwords, or other authentication information in the content of a support request. Choose an appropriate severity: choosing an inappropriate severity level may lead to unexpected response times or slow down resolution. After creating a request, regularly check AWS Support Center to update information and respond promptly to questions from the support team. Week 2 Achievements: Understood the role of AWS Budgets in cost control and the 4 budget types:
Cost Budget Usage Budget RI Budget Savings Plans Budget Distinguished Reserved Instances from Savings Plans and understood why Savings Plans is preferred for EC2.
Learned how to access AWS Billing and Cost Management and create budgets in 2 ways:
Using a template (Monthly cost budget) Customized, with full settings: period, recurring/expiring, fixed/planned, scope, aggregate costs Practiced creating a Cost Budget and a Usage Budget (tracking EC2 running hours), configuring alert thresholds and notification emails.
Learned to monitor Budget health and Budget history to evaluate usage against the budget.
Understood the process of creating an RI Budget and a Savings Plans Budget.
Learned how to clean up budgets after practice and understood that deleting a budget does not affect running resources.
Understood that budgets only send alerts and do not automatically block resource usage.
Learned the 4 AWS Support plans (Basic, Business Support+, Enterprise Support, Unified Operations), with the features and response times of each.
Understood the process of managing support requests in AWS Support Center, the importance of choosing the right severity, and the security considerations when creating a support case.

title: Proposal
content:
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? The Solution Benefits and Return on Investment 3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

title: Week 3 Worklog
content:
Week 3 Objectives: Understand the role of AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) in access control and know its main components: User, Group, Policy, Role. Practice creating IAM Groups, IAM Users, IAM Roles, and switching roles following the principle of least privilege. Understand Amazon VPC: CIDR, subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway. Distinguish Security Groups from Network ACLs, and understand VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer. Grasp the architecture of a multi-AZ VPC deployment with EC2, NAT Gateway, Session Manager, and CloudWatch monitoring. Understand the AWS Site-to-Site VPN model (Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, tunnels) and know how to clean up resources in the right order to avoid costs. Learn the resource clean-up order and Infrastructure as Code templates (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) - Summarize week 3 knowledge and write the worklog 23/10/2026 23/10/2026 https://000003.awsfcaj.com/3-prerequisite/ https://000003.awsfcaj.com/4-createec2server/ https://000003.awsfcaj.com/5-vpnsitetosite/ https://000003.awsfcaj.com/6-cleanup/ https://000003.awsfcaj.com/7-infrastructureascode/ Practice and learning details: Lab 2: Managing Access Control with AWS IAM 1. IAM overview
IAM is a security service for centrally managing access to AWS services and resources: creating user identities, fine-grained permissions, and secure authentication. The root user has full access to everything in the account: protect it with a strong password and MFA, do not use it for daily tasks, and create IAM users with appropriate permissions instead; use root only for specific tasks. Three core features: Shared account access without sharing credentials. Granular access control per user and per resource, following least privilege and custom policies. Secure application access: manage credentials for applications on EC2 and use IAM roles for service-to-service communication. Security features: MFA, identity federation with external providers, CloudTrail integration for auditing, PCI DSS compliance support, eventual consistency model. Three access methods: AWS Management Console, command line tools (AWS CLI, PowerShell), programmatic access (AWS SDKs, IAM Query API over HTTPS). AWS CloudShell provides command-line access from the console with no local install. Cost: IAM and AWS STS are free; you only pay for the other AWS services you use. Four core components: IAM User: an individual identity with long-term credentials. IAM Group: a collection of users. IAM Policy: permission definitions in JSON. IAM Role: temporary credentials for service-to-service access or for trusted entities. 2. Create IAM Group and IAM User
Create an IAM Group and configure administrative permissions. Create a new IAM User and add it to the administrative group. Set up secure login credentials and sign in to the AWS account as the Admin User to verify administrative access. Notes: document and securely store the credentials since later labs need them; manage permissions through groups rather than attaching policies to individual users. 3. Create IAM Role and IAM User
Roles provide temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys and delegate permissions to trusted entities (IAM users in your account or AWS services). Using roles rather than direct policy attachments gives better control and simpler management. Objectives: Create an IAM Role named Admin with the AdministratorAccess managed policy. Create an IAM User named OperatorUser. Configure role-assumption permissions for OperatorUser. Warning: AdministratorAccess grants full access; follow your organization’s security policies when assigning administrative permissions. 4. Switch Role
Switching roles means temporarily assuming a previously created role, including across AWS accounts, using temporary credentials instead of long-term keys, which fits least privilege. Steps: (1) configure role-switch permissions for OperatorUser, (2) access the AWS Console as OperatorUser, (3) perform the role switch. Prerequisites: completed the admin group/user section and the Admin role/OperatorUser section. Tip: after finishing work in the assumed role, switch back to your original role to keep audit trails clear and prevent unintended resource access. 5. Clean up resources
Open the IAM Console, choose Users, select the lab user, choose Delete, and confirm in the dialog. Choose User groups, select the lab group, choose Delete, and confirm. Check the IAM Dashboard to confirm all lab resources are gone. General security tips: use IAM Roles for temporary permissions instead of direct assignments, set session timeouts, monitor access activity through AWS CloudTrail, and regularly review permissions following least privilege.
Lab 3: Amazon VPC and AWS Site-to-Site VPN 1. Introduction to Amazon VPC
A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network in AWS where you launch EC2, ECS/EKS, RDS and similar resources while controlling the network configuration; it is built on the AWS Nitro System. Key capabilities: IP management: primary and secondary IPv4 CIDRs, native IPv6, Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM). Segmentation: public, private, isolated and IPv6-only subnets across multiple AZs. Routing and gateways: route tables, Internet Gateway, Egress-Only Internet Gateway (IPv6), NAT Gateway. Hybrid and multi-VPC connectivity: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN. Security: Security Groups (stateful), Network ACLs (stateless), AWS Network Firewall. IP addressing: IPv4 CIDR block sizes range from /16 (65,536 addresses) to /28 (16 addresses); the primary CIDR cannot be modified after creation; up to 4 secondary CIDR blocks can be added. VPC CIDRs must not overlap with on-premises subnets, peered VPCs or transit networks. The default VPC is 172.31.0.0/16, with a public subnet in each AZ. IPv6 allocation is /56 per VPC and /64 per subnet. Cost note: since 1 Feb 2024, AWS charges $0.005 per hour for every public IPv4 address. Use custom VPCs rather than the default VPC in production to apply least privilege, build multi-tier subnets (Public, Application, Database) and avoid CIDR conflicts. Observability components: VPC Flow Logs (capture IP traffic metadata, delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Kinesis Data Firehose) and VPC Reachability Analyzer (verifies paths between resources without sending packets). 2. Firewalls in VPC
Security Group: A virtual firewall at the instance (ENI) level, stateful: return traffic is automatically allowed. Each instance can have up to 5 Security Groups. By default all outbound traffic is allowed and all inbound is denied. Rules can reference other Security Groups, AWS services or IP ranges. Network ACL (NACL): An optional subnet-level firewall, stateless: explicit rules must be defined for both inbound and outbound traffic. Each subnet is associated with exactly one NACL (default or custom); rules are evaluated in numerical order, lowest number first. The default NACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic. The two layers complement each other: Security Groups give fine-grained instance-level control while NACLs give broader subnet-level protection. 3. Preparation Steps
Goal: build a multi-AZ VPC with public and private subnets following AWS best practices. Order: create VPC → create Subnets → create Internet Gateway → create Route Tables → create Security Groups → enable VPC Flow Logs (the VPC Resource Map can be used to view the structure). Cost note: most VPC components are free but NAT Gateways incur charges. The workshop creates each component individually (instead of using the VPC Wizard) to show how they fit together. 4. Deploying Amazon EC2 Instances
Multi-AZ architecture, highly available NAT Gateways, secure access (SSH and Session Manager), CloudWatch monitoring and alerting, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Order: create EC2 server → test connection → create NAT Gateway → use Reachability Analyzer → create EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint (optional) → AWS Systems Manager Session Manager → CloudWatch Monitoring & Alerting. The prerequisite is having enabled VPC Flow Logs. Resources used in the lab: EC2 Public, EC2 Private, NAT-Gateway (NAT-Gateway-AZ1a, NAT-Gateway-AZ1b), and the VPC endpoints for Session Manager: SSM-Endpoint, SSM Messages Endpoint, EC2 Messages Endpoint. 5. Setting up AWS Site-to-Site VPN
Site-to-Site VPN connects an on-premises data center to Amazon VPC. Concepts: Virtual Private Gateway (VPG): the AWS-side tunnel termination point. Customer Gateway (CGW): represents the customer’s VPN device (hardware or software). BGP: dynamic routing if the CGW supports it; otherwise use static routing and enter the routes yourself. IPsec: the protocol creating the secure tunnel over the internet. Each VPN connection has 2 tunnels for high availability; connections are initiated from the CGW to the VPG. Steps: set up the VPG → set up the CGW → choose BGP or static routing → the tunnel comes up when traffic flows. Lab scenario: the main office is the VPC ASG (10.10.0.0/16) and the branch office is the VPC ASG VPN (10.11.0.0/16), in different Availability Zones. Initially both sides allow external SSH but the instances cannot ping each other by private IP; the goal is private-IP connectivity across the VPN. The customer is responsible for preparing the internet connection. 6. Clean up resources
Delete resources in dependency order to avoid errors and stop charges: EC2 instances: EC2 Public, EC2 Private, EC2 Customer Gateway (if created) → Instance state → Terminate instance. NAT Gateways: NAT-Gateway, NAT-Gateway-AZ1a, NAT-Gateway-AZ1b → Actions → Delete NAT gateway, type delete; wait for the Deleted status (about 5-10 minutes). Elastic IPs: Actions → Release Elastic IP addresses. VPC endpoints: SSM-Endpoint, SSM Messages Endpoint, EC2 Messages Endpoint → Actions → Delete VPC endpoints. VPN resources (if applicable): delete the Site-to-Site VPN connection (wait 2-5 minutes); detach then delete the Virtual Private Gateway; delete the Customer Gateway. VPCs: delete ASG VPN first, then ASG → Actions → Delete VPC, type delete. Approximate costs: NAT Gateway $0.045/hour plus $0.045/GB processed; unused Elastic IP $0.005/hour; VPN connection $0.05/hour. Notes: instance store data is lost on termination; EBS volumes may remain if “Delete on Termination” is off; CloudWatch Logs, EBS snapshots and S3 buckets may still incur charges and must be deleted separately. Verify with the Billing Dashboard, Cost Explorer and Bills, and set Budget Alerts. 7. Infrastructure as Code
IaC provides repeatability, version control, automation, standardization, uniform security policy, and audit trails. The workshop provides 3 templates that create a multi-AZ 10.10.0.0/16 VPC with public/private subnets, 2 NAT Gateways, route tables, security groups, SSM VPC endpoints, and VPC Flow Logs: CloudFormation (YAML): parameters VpcCidr and Environment (dev, staging, prod); deployed with aws cloudformation create-stack. AWS CDK (TypeScript): stack ProductionVpcStack; deployed with cdk bootstrap and cdk deploy. Terraform: file terraform/main.tf; deployed with terraform init, plan, apply. Best practices: do not open SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 in production, use Secrets Manager or Parameter Store for secrets, least-privilege IAM, encryption, multi-AZ deployment, CI/CD, and separate dev/staging/prod environments. Week 3 Achievements: Understood the role of IAM and distinguished its 4 components:
IAM User IAM Group IAM Policy IAM Role Understood why the root user should not be used for daily tasks and why MFA should be enabled.
Learned the permission management workflow: create an admin group, create a user, assign permissions through the group; create the Admin role with AdministratorAccess, create OperatorUser, and use Switch Role to assume temporary permissions.
Understood the principle of least privilege, the preference for roles with temporary credentials, and how to clean up users/groups after practice.
Understood the Amazon VPC structure: CIDR, public/private/isolated subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, IPv6 and IPAM.
Distinguished Security Groups (stateful, instance level) from Network ACLs (stateless, subnet level, rules evaluated in order).
Understood the role of VPC Flow Logs and VPC Reachability Analyzer in network monitoring and troubleshooting.
Learned the process of building a multi-AZ VPC and deploying EC2 with NAT Gateway, Session Manager, and CloudWatch.
Understood the AWS Site-to-Site VPN model: VPG, CGW, BGP/static routing, 2 IPsec tunnels.
Learned the VPC resource clean-up order (EC2 → NAT Gateway → Elastic IP → VPC endpoint → VPN → VPC) and the costs that accumulate easily, such as NAT Gateways, Elastic IPs, public IPv4 addresses, and VPN connections.
Became aware of Infrastructure as Code templates (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) for automated VPC deployment.

title: Week 4 Worklog
content:
Week 4 Objectives: Understand Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) and its core features: instance types, AMIs, EBS, key pairs, security groups, Elastic IP. Prepare the networking infrastructure (VPC, security groups), then launch and connect to EC2 instances running Windows Server 2025 and Amazon Linux 2023. Practice basic EC2 operations: changing the instance type, EBS snapshots, creating and sharing a custom AMI, recovering access when a key pair is lost. Deploy the Node.js “AWS User Management” (CRUD) application on Linux (LAMP + Node.js) and Windows (XAMPP + Node.js). Apply IAM to manage costs and limit EC2 usage (by region, instance family, instance type, EBS volume type, IP address, and time period). Understand how to grant an application access to AWS services: using access keys (to be avoided) versus an IAM Role attached to EC2 (recommended). Clean up resources in the right order to avoid costs. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Learn the Amazon EC2 overview: + Concepts and use cases + Instance types, AMIs, storage options (EBS, instance store) + Security and access: key pairs, security groups, NACLs, IAM roles, Session Manager + Features: Auto Scaling, Load Balancing, Elastic IP, Placement Groups, multiple AZs - Practice (Preparation): + Create a VPC for the Linux instance and a VPC for the Windows instance + Create a Security Group for Linux and one for Windows 26/10/2026 26/10/2026 https://000004.awsfcaj.com/ https://000004.awsfcaj.com/1-introduce/ https://000004.awsfcaj.com/2-prerequiste/ 3 - Practice: + Launch a Microsoft Windows Server 2025 instance and connect from the computer (Remote Desktop) + Launch an Amazon Linux instance and connect (SSH) - Take note: running instances keep incurring charges and must be terminated when no longer needed; remote access depends on the security group configuration 27/10/2026 27/10/2026 https://000004.awsfcaj.com/3-launchwindowsinstance/ https://000004.awsfcaj.com/4-launchlinuxinstance/ 4 - Practice Amazon EC2 Basic: + Modify the instance type + Create and manage EBS snapshots + Create a Custom AMI and launch an instance from it + Recover access to a Windows instance (using Systems Manager) and a Linux instance (using user data) when the key pair is lost + Remote Desktop to EC2 Ubuntu + (Optional) EBS Snapshots Archive and Share AMI 28/10/2026 28/10/2026 https://000004.awsfcaj.com/5-amazonec2basic/ 5 - Deploy the AWS User Management application (Node.js, Express, Express-Handlebars, MySQL): + Linux (Amazon Linux 2023): install LAMP (prepare, test, configure/secure the database, install phpMyAdmin), install Node.js, deploy the application + Windows (Windows Server 2025): install XAMPP, install Node.js, deploy the application + Open inbound ports in the security group (3000 for the application, 80 for XAMPP) and test the CRUD functions 29/10/2026 29/10/2026 https://000004.awsfcaj.com/6-awsfcjmanagement-linux/ https://000004.awsfcaj.com/7-awsfcjmanagement-windows/ 6 - Cost and usage governance with IAM: restrict services by region; limit EC2 by instance family and instance type; manage EBS volume types; limit delete permissions by company IP and by time period - IAM Role for EC2 workshop: create EC2 and an S3 bucket; use an IAM user’s access key (not recommended); use an IAM role attached to EC2 (recommended) - Clean up both workshops - Summarize week 4 knowledge and write the worklog 30/10/2026 30/10/2026 https://000004.awsfcaj.com/8-costusagegovernance/ https://000004.awsfcaj.com/9-cleanup/ https://000048.awsfcaj.com/ https://000048.awsfcaj.com/4-cleanup/ Practice and learning details: Lab 4: Introduction to Amazon EC2 1. Amazon EC2 overview
Amazon EC2 provides on-demand, scalable compute capacity in the AWS Cloud, letting you launch virtual servers without upfront hardware investment. Use cases include web hosting, applications, databases, authentication services, and enterprise tasks. You can launch or stop any number of virtual servers, configure security and networking, manage storage, and scale capacity up or down. Instance type: defines the hardware configuration of the virtual server and must be chosen when launching an instance. CPUs: Intel, AMD, AWS Graviton (ARM) and GPU; RAM varies by instance family; network performance ranges from moderate to 100+ Gbps. Families: C (compute-optimized, e.g., batch processing), R (memory-optimized, e.g., databases), T and M (general-purpose). AMI (Amazon Machine Image): contains the operating system and configuration, application server and applications, launch permissions, and block device mapping. Options are AWS-provided AMIs, AWS Marketplace AMIs, and custom AMIs created from existing instances. Storage: EBS volume: persistent, network-attached storage independent of the instance lifecycle. Instance store: temporary storage physically attached to the host; data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated. Security and access: key pairs (SSH), security groups (virtual firewalls), NACLs (stateless packet filtering at the subnet level), IAM roles (grant permissions to applications running on EC2), Systems Manager Session Manager (access without opening inbound SSH/RDP ports or distributing private keys). Key features: Elastic infrastructure: EC2 Auto Scaling, Elastic Load Balancing, dynamic attach/detach of resources. Networking: VPC, Elastic IP (static IPv4), Placement Groups. High availability: multiple Availability Zones, Local Zones, AWS Outposts, Wavelength Zones. Resource management: Tags, Resource Groups, CloudFormation. Monitoring: CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Systems Manager. Tips: match the instance family to the workload to balance performance and cost; store data that must persist on EBS, not on instance store; associate Elastic IPs with running instances or release them when unused to avoid charges. The workshop was tested on Microsoft Windows Server 2025 and Amazon Linux 2023 (plus Ubuntu), using the sample Node.js application AWS User Management with CRUD functionality. 2. Preparation
Before launching EC2, set up networking and security controls: VPC: an isolated network for the instances; created separately for the Linux (2.1) and Windows (2.2) environments. Security Group: a stateful virtual firewall controlling inbound and outbound traffic; created separately for Linux (2.3) and Windows (2.4). Note: a misconfigured VPC or security group can block legitimate traffic or expose instances. Security groups should allow only the traffic the application needs and block other access. 3. Launch and connect to Windows Server 2025 / Amazon Linux
Windows Server 2025: Microsoft’s newest server release with stronger security and better performance; AWS offers it through license-included AMIs, integrated with Systems Manager and Active Directory. Two parts: launching the instance (3.1) and connecting from the computer (3.2). Amazon Linux: the AWS-provided Linux distribution aimed at a secure, stable, high-performance environment for EC2 applications. Launching the instance (4.1) and connecting (4.2). Cost warning: running instances keep incurring charges, so terminate them when no longer needed. Security note: remote access (RDP/SSH) depends on a properly configured security group. 4. Amazon EC2 Basic
Basic operations with EC2 and its components, including changing configurations and recovering access when a key pair is lost:
5.1 Modify EC2 Instance Type: change the instance type of an instance. 5.2 Create and Manage EBS Snapshots: create and manage snapshots of EBS volumes. 5.3 Create Custom AMI: create a custom AMI from an instance. 5.4 Launch an Instance from a Custom AMI: launch a new instance from the created AMI. 5.5 Recovering Access to Windows Instances: recover access to a Windows instance using AWS Systems Manager when the key pair is lost. 5.6 Recovering Access to Linux Instances: recover access to a Linux instance using user data when the key pair is lost. 5.7 Remote Desktop to EC2-Ubuntu: connect by remote desktop to an EC2 Ubuntu instance. 5.8 Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive (optional): archive snapshots for long-term storage. 5.9 Share AMI (optional): share an AMI. Security note: manage key pairs securely and know the alternative access methods. These operations help build resilient architectures and manage compute resources efficiently. 5. Deploying the AWS User Management application on Amazon Linux 2023
The application uses Node.js, Express, Express-Handlebars and MySQL, and provides a CRUD interface to manage users. Prerequisites: an EC2 instance running Amazon Linux 2023, basic AWS and Linux knowledge, an AWS account with appropriate permissions. Steps: Install LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP): prepare the LAMP server (6.1.1), test the LAMP server (6.1.2), configure and secure the database server (6.1.3), install phpMyAdmin (6.1.4). Install Node.js (6.2). Deploy the application (6.3): clone the repository, install dependencies with npm, configure the database connection, start the server, and test the CRUD functions. Tip: when configuring MariaDB/MySQL, run mysql_secure_installation to set a strong root password and remove test databases. In production, use the latest LTS version of Node.js to get the most recent security patches. Warning: the EC2 security group must allow inbound traffic on the application’s port (typically 3000) so it can be reached from a browser. 6. Deploying Node.js applications on Amazon EC2 Windows
Deploy the same AWS User Management application on Windows Server 2025 Base. Steps: Install XAMPP (MySQL/MariaDB, Apache, PHP) as the database environment (7.1). Configure the database schema through phpMyAdmin. Install Node.js (7.2). Deploy and configure the application (7.3). Test the CRUD operations. Warning: the security group must allow inbound traffic on port 80 (XAMPP) and port 3000 (the Node.js app). Tip: XAMPP simplifies installing MySQL, Apache and PHP on Windows, which suits development and testing; for production, use Amazon RDS for MySQL instead of a local database for better scalability, reliability and security. 7. Cost and usage governance with IAM
IAM offers fine-grained access control that supports both security and cost governance. EC2’s flexibility makes it quick to deploy environments like XAMPP and LAMP, but that flexibility needs governance. Least-privilege IAM policies strengthen security and support cost optimization by preventing unauthorized resource provisioning; well-designed policies prevent both over-provisioning (waste) and under-provisioning (limited performance). Six practice topics: 8.1 Restrict service usage by AWS Region. 8.2 Limit EC2 usage by instance family. 8.3 Control EC2 deployment by instance type. 8.4 Manage the allowed EBS volume types. 8.5 Limit permission to delete resources by the company’s IP address. 8.6 Limit permission to delete resources by time period. 8. Clean up resources (EC2 workshop)
In this order:
Terminate EC2 instances: EC2 → Instances → select the lab instances → Instance state → Terminate instance. Deregister AMIs: EC2 → AMIs → select the created AMI → Actions → Deregister AMI. Delete EBS snapshots: EC2 → Snapshots → select the lab snapshots → Actions → Delete snapshot. Delete Security Groups: EC2 → Security Groups → Actions → Delete security group (make sure the group is not attached to any running instance). Delete Key Pairs: EC2 → Key Pairs → select the lab key pair → Actions → Delete. Delete the VPC: VPC → Your VPCs → select the lab VPC → Actions → Delete VPC (deleting the VPC also removes its subnets, route tables, internet gateways and NAT gateways). Delete IAM resources: User Groups, Users, Policies, Roles. Lab 48: Granting an Application Access to AWS Services with an IAM Role 1. Objectives and architecture
The workshop covers two ways to give an application access to AWS services: Access keys (access key ID and secret access key) of an IAM user: how it works and why it should be avoided. An IAM role attached to EC2: the recommended approach. Services used: AWS IAM (user, access key, role), Amazon EC2 (hosts the application, the role attaches to it) and Amazon S3 (the bucket the application accesses). Scenario: a Python application running on EC2 uploads an object to an S3 bucket, first using an access key and then using an IAM role. 2. Preparation
1.1 Create EC2 Instance: launch the EC2 instance that runs the application. 1.2 Create S3 bucket: create the S3 bucket the application will access. 3. Using an access key (not recommended)
2.1 Generate IAM user and access key: create an IAM user and generate its access key ID and secret access key. 2.2 Use access key: use the access key in the Python application to upload an object to the S3 bucket. An access key is a long-term credential that has to be stored in the application/server, so it is easily exposed. 4. Using an IAM role on EC2 (recommended)
3.1 Create IAM role: create an IAM role with permissions for the required service (the role in the lab is EC2RoleS3Upload). 3.2 Using IAM role: attach the role to the EC2 instance and confirm the application can upload files to S3 without storing any key. 5. Clean up (IAM Role workshop)
Delete the S3 bucket (region us-east-1): select the bucket s3-instancerole-xxxx → Empty → type permanently delete → Empty; then select the bucket again → Delete → enter the bucket name → Delete bucket. Terminate the EC2 instance: EC2 → Instances → select the lab instance → Instance state → Terminate instance → Terminate. Delete the IAM user IAMAccessKey: IAM → Users → select the user → Delete → choose to deactivate the access key → type confirm → Delete user. Delete the IAM role EC2RoleS3Upload: IAM → Roles → search ec2 → select the role → Delete → enter the role name → Delete. Week 4 Achievements: Understood Amazon EC2 and its main components:
Instance types and families (C, R, T, M) AMIs EBS volumes and instance store Key pairs, security groups, NACLs Elastic IP and high-availability features (multiple AZs, Auto Scaling, Load Balancing) Learned the process of preparing a separate VPC and security group for the Linux and Windows environments before creating instances.
Learned how to launch and connect to Windows Server 2025 and Amazon Linux 2023.
Learned the basic EC2 operations: changing the instance type, EBS snapshots, Custom AMIs, launching from an AMI, sharing an AMI, EBS Snapshots Archive, and the ways to recover access when a key pair is lost.
Understood how to deploy a Node.js application (Express, Express-Handlebars, MySQL) on Linux (LAMP + Node.js) and Windows (XAMPP + Node.js), and the ports to open in the security group (3000 and 80).
Understood why production should use Amazon RDS for MySQL instead of a local database, and should use the LTS version of Node.js.
Understood how to use IAM to manage costs: limits by region, instance family, instance type, EBS volume type, IP address, and time period.
Distinguished the two ways of granting an application access to AWS services and understood why an IAM Role attached to EC2 is preferred over long-term access keys.
Learned the EC2 resource clean-up order (instance → AMI → snapshot → security group → key pair → VPC → IAM) and how to clean up the IAM Role workshop resources (S3 bucket, EC2, IAM user, IAM role).

title: Workshop
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS. title: Sharing and Feedback
content:

Here, you can freely share your personal opinions about your experience participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program. This will help the FCAJ team improve any shortcomings based on the following aspects:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The working environment is very friendly and open. FCAJ members are always willing to help whenever I encounter difficulties, even outside working hours. The workspace is tidy and comfortable, helping me focus better. However, I think it would be nice to have more social gatherings or team bonding activities to strengthen relationships.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentor provides very detailed guidance, explains clearly when I don’t understand, and always encourages me to ask questions. The admin team supports administrative tasks, provides necessary documents, and creates favorable conditions for me to work effectively. I especially appreciate that the mentor allows me to try and solve problems myself instead of just giving the answer.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
The tasks I was assigned align well with the knowledge I learned at university, while also introducing me to new areas I had never encountered before. This allowed me to both strengthen my foundational knowledge and gain practical skills.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
During the internship, I learned many new skills such as using project management tools, teamwork skills, and professional communication in a corporate environment. The mentor also shared valuable real-world experiences that helped me better plan my career path.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
The company culture is very positive: everyone respects each other, works seriously but still keeps things enjoyable. When there are urgent projects, everyone works together and supports one another regardless of their position. This made me feel like a real part of the team, even as an intern.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits
The company provides an internship allowance and offers flexible working hours when needed. In addition, having the opportunity to join internal training sessions is a big plus.
